title: Principal components from the SVD
summary: Principal component analysis (PCA) by hand on five points: centring, variance along a direction, the covariance matrix, the top eigenvector as the best direction, the same answer from the SVD, and what keeping one component loses.
written: Written by Claude Code (Opus 5.5) on 15 Nov 2026, after the least-squares course and docs/seed-context.md. One data set throughout, designed and checked in sympy first. Every answer key is re-derived with sympy by tools/validate_courses.py.

sources.name: Mark's notes and chats (seed context)
sources.note: docs/seed-context.md: PCA not yet taught; SVD, the pseudo-inverse and Eckart–Young already worked; he compares guesses before optimising; his slips (non-symmetric AᵀA, transposed rows, sums, scale factors).

sources.name: Principal component analysis (Wikipedia)
sources.note: Centre the columns first; covariance with 1/(n − 1); principal directions as the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix and as the right singular vectors of X, with eigenvalues the squared singular values; scores T = XW = UΣ; explained variance as an eigenvalue over their sum; truncation as the best low-rank approximation (Eckart–Young, Frobenius norm).

sources.name: Jonathon Shlens, A Tutorial on Principal Component Analysis (arXiv:1404.1100)
sources.note: Subtract each measurement's mean, then use the covariance with 1/(n − 1); the eigenvector route and the SVD route to the same principal components. (Shlens puts measurements in rows; this course puts points in rows, as Wikipedia does.)

sources.name: Gilbert Strang, MIT 18.065 (Spring 2018), Lecture 7: Eckart–Young, with a review of PCA
sources.note: From the lecture transcript: centre the data, divide by n − 1 for the sample covariance, the best line minimises perpendicular distances where least squares minimises vertical ones, and Eckart–Young holds in the 2-norm and the Frobenius norm.

lessons.title: Spread along a direction
lessons.summary: Centre five points, then compare how far they spread along a few guessed directions.

lessons.title: The covariance matrix
lessons.summary: C = XᵀX/(n − 1): every variance from one symmetric 2×2 matrix.

lessons.title: The best direction is an eigenvector
lessons.summary: The eigenvector of C with the largest eigenvalue spreads the points most, and its line is the closest to them.

lessons.title: The same answer from the SVD
lessons.summary: The SVD of the centred data gives the directions, the variances σ²/(n − 1) and the scores.

lessons.title: Keeping one component
lessons.summary: Rebuild each point from one number, measure what is lost, and meet Eckart–Young again.
